vignette: John, a 50-year-old psychologist, had spent his career helping others navigate the intricacies of the mind, but he found himself ensnared in a web of trauma that he could no longer unravel alone. One fateful night, after a gathering with colleagues, John had been assaulted. The incident had left him reeling, and as the weeks turned into months, he found himself unable to escape the haunting reminders of that night. The smell of alcohol became a potent trigger, transporting him back to a place he desperately wanted to forget. Every time John caught a whiff of it, he couldn't shake the thought that he was forever marked by that night, reinforcing the belief that he was weak and incapable of moving forward. Each time he caught a whiff of it, a wave of discomfort washed over him, making him acutely aware of his vulnerability. This discomfort deepened his negative self-appraisal, leading him to believe that he was permanently marked by the trauma, a belief that made him feel weak and incapable of moving forward. The conviction that he was no longer the man he once was kept drawing him back to the traumatic memories, as if he needed to find proof of his perceived failures in the vividness of those recollections. This discomfort compounded his negative self-appraisal, leading him to believe that his vulnerability was a permanent state, a confirmation of his incapacity to cope with life. The sound of sirens, too, became an unbearable reminder of the chaos that had engulfed him. It was as if every auditory signal in his environment conspired to pull him back into that moment of fear and helplessness. As John navigated his daily life, he felt an overwhelming sense of emotional numbness. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of the things that once defined him - his passion for psychology had dulled, and he felt like a mere shadow of the person he used to be. He often described himself as feeling "dead inside," as though he had been reduced to an object rather than a person with thoughts and feelings. This dehumanization seeped into his interactions, making him feel disconnected from those he loved, especially his wife. As he grappled with the belief that he had lost his essence, memories of the traumatic night would intrude, reinforcing the idea that he was no longer the man he once was. Each time the memories surfaced, they were accompanied by a harsh internal dialogue that echoed his belief that he was broken, making him feel even more entrenched in his negative self-view. John's negative self-appraisal was so profound that he struggled to articulate his experiences, often pushing the memories away before he could fully confront them. He would sit in silence, feeling the emotional intensity of that night without the ability to frame it in words, leaving him trapped in a cycle of confusion and despair. The interplay between John's memories and his negative appraisals deepened his distress. Every time he attempted to recall that night, the emotional weight felt insurmountable, reinforcing his belief that he had lost the essence of who he was. It was as if the trauma had created a chasm between his past and present self, one that he could not bridge. The memories floated just out of reach, and yet the feelings associated with them were vivid and intense, leaving him feeling raw and exposed. In those moments, he would often think that if he couldn't control these memories, it meant there was something fundamentally wrong with him, reinforcing the belief that he was broken. The conviction that he was no longer the man he once was kept drawing him back to that night, each recollection weighted with the belief that he had irrevocably changed for the worse. Each time the memories resurfaced, they were accompanied by a harsh internal dialogue that echoed the belief that he was weak, leading him to conclude that he had irrevocably changed for the worse. This inability to articulate his trauma contributed to his pervasive sense of being an object rather than a person, further entrenching his negative self-view and heightening his sensitivity to triggers in his environment. Every time the memories resurfaced, they reinforced the belief that he was broken, leading him to think that he could never reclaim the life he once had or the person he used to be. John's relationship with his wife had suffered immensely as a result of these spiraling thoughts. He increasingly withdrew from her, avoiding shared social occasions that might involve alcohol or where sirens could be heard in the distance. The belief that he was failing his wife compounded his fear of these situations, convincing him that any moment could expose his vulnerability, which only heightened his sensitivity to potential triggers around him. Each avoidance act, while providing temporary relief, only deepened his feelings of isolation and hopelessness. "His negative appraisal of himself made every act of avoidance feel like a confirmation of his incapacity, feeding into a cycle where the world seemed more threatening and his ability to cope was diminished." vignette_attempts.vignette:
John, a 50-year-old psychologist, had spent his career helping others navigate the intricacies of the mind, but he found himself ensnared in a web of trauma that he could no longer unravel alone. One fateful night, after a gathering with colleagues, John had been assaulted. The incident had left him reeling, and as the weeks turned into months, he found himself unable to escape the haunting reminders of that night. The smell of alcohol became a potent trigger, transporting him back to a place he desperately wanted to forget. Each time he caught a whiff of it, a wave of discomfort washed over him, making him acutely aware of his vulnerability. The sound of sirens, too, became an unbearable reminder of the chaos that had engulfed him. It was as if every auditory signal in his environment conspired to pull him back into that moment of fear and helplessness.

As John navigated his daily life, he felt an overwhelming sense of emotional numbness. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of the things that once defined him — his passion for psychology had dulled, and he felt like a mere shadow of the person he used to be. He often described himself as feeling “dead inside,” as though he had been reduced to an object rather than a person with thoughts and feelings. This dehumanization seeped into his interactions, making him feel disconnected from those he loved, especially his wife. John’s negative self-appraisal was so profound that he struggled to articulate his experiences, often pushing the memories away before he could fully confront them. He would sit in silence, feeling the emotional intensity of that night without the ability to frame it in words, leaving him trapped in a cycle of confusion and despair.

The interplay between John’s memories and his negative appraisals deepened his distress. Every time he attempted to recall that night, the emotional weight felt insurmountable, reinforcing his belief that he had lost the essence of who he was. It was as if the trauma had created a chasm between his past and present self, one that he could not bridge. The memories floated just out of reach, and yet the feelings associated with them were vivid and intense, leaving him feeling raw and exposed. This inability to articulate his trauma contributed to his pervasive sense of being an object rather than a person, further entrenching his negative self-view and heightening his sensitivity to triggers in his environment.

John’s relationship with his wife had suffered immensely as a result of these spiraling thoughts. He increasingly withdrew from her, avoiding shared social occasions that might involve alcohol or where sirens could be heard in the distance. Each avoidance act, while providing temporary relief, only deepened his feelings of isolation and hopelessness. He felt the weight of his inaction, believing that he was failing not just himself but also his partner, whom he loved dearly. This compounded his feelings of shame and unworthiness, reinforcing the deep-seated belief that he was no longer capable of being the husband she deserved. Each time he avoided a potential trigger, he felt guilty, convinced that he was becoming a burden rather than a companion.

After months of struggling with these issues, John finally sought help. He had come to realize that the pain of remaining silent was far greater than the fear of confronting his past. Yet, what frightened him most was the possibility that he would never be able to reclaim the person he once was — a capable, compassionate psychologist and a loving husband. In his heart, he clung to a flicker of hope that therapy might help him navigate through the memories that haunted him, allowing him to transform his pain into a path toward healing and reconnection with those he loved.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not establish a causal connection where triggers influence negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals lead to intrusive memories.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette fails to demonstrate how memory influences negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."

vignette_attempts.vignette: John, a 50-year-old psychologist, had spent his career helping others navigate the intricacies of the mind, but he found himself ensnared in a web of trauma that he could no longer unravel alone. One fateful night, after a gathering with colleagues, John had been assaulted. The incident had left him reeling, and as the weeks turned into months, he found himself unable to escape the haunting reminders of that night. The smell of alcohol became a potent trigger, transporting him back to a place he desperately wanted to forget. Every time John caught a whiff of it, he couldn’t shake the thought that he was forever marked by that night, reinforcing the belief that he was weak and incapable of moving forward. Each time he caught a whiff of it, a wave of discomfort washed over him, making him acutely aware of his vulnerability. This discomfort deepened his negative self-appraisal, leading him to believe that he was permanently marked by the trauma, a belief that made him feel weak and incapable of moving forward. The conviction that he was no longer the man he once was kept drawing him back to the traumatic memories, as if he needed to find proof of his perceived failures in the vividness of those recollections. This discomfort compounded his negative self-appraisal, leading him to believe that his vulnerability was a permanent state, a confirmation of his incapacity to cope with life. The sound of sirens, too, became an unbearable reminder of the chaos that had engulfed him. It was as if every auditory signal in his environment conspired to pull him back into that moment of fear and helplessness. As John navigated his daily life, he felt an overwhelming sense of emotional numbness. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of the things that once defined him — his passion for psychology had dulled, and he felt like a mere shadow of the person he used to be. He often described himself as feeling “dead inside,” as though he had been reduced to an object rather than a person with thoughts and feelings. This dehumanization seeped into his interactions, making him feel disconnected from those he loved, especially his wife. As he grappled with the belief that he had lost his essence, memories of the traumatic night would intrude, reinforcing the idea that he was no longer the man he once was. Each time the memories surfaced, they were accompanied by a harsh internal dialogue that echoed his belief that he was broken, making him feel even more entrenched in his negative self-view. John’s negative self-appraisal was so profound that he struggled to articulate his experiences, often pushing the memories away before he could fully confront them. He would sit in silence, feeling the emotional intensity of that night without the ability to frame it in words, leaving him trapped in a cycle of confusion and despair. The interplay between John’s memories and his negative appraisals deepened his distress. Every time he attempted to recall that night, the emotional weight felt insurmountable, reinforcing his belief that he had lost the essence of who he was. It was as if the trauma had created a chasm between his past and present self, one that he could not bridge. The memories floated just out of reach, and yet the feelings associated with them were vivid and intense, leaving him feeling raw and exposed. In those moments, he would often think that if he couldn’t control these memories, it meant there was something fundamentally wrong with him, reinforcing the belief that he was broken. The conviction that he was no longer the man he once was kept drawing him back to that night, each recollection weighted with the belief that he had irrevocably changed for the worse. Each time the memories resurfaced, they were accompanied by a harsh internal dialogue that echoed the belief that he was weak, leading him to conclude that he had irrevocably changed for the worse. This inability to articulate his trauma contributed to his pervasive sense of being an object rather than a person, further entrenching his negative self-view and heightening his sensitivity to triggers in his environment. Every time the memories resurfaced, they reinforced the belief that he was broken, leading him to think that he could never reclaim the life he once had or the person he used to be. John’s relationship with his wife had suffered immensely as a result of these spiraling thoughts. He increasingly withdrew from her, avoiding shared social occasions that might involve alcohol or where sirens could be heard in the distance. The belief that he was failing his wife compounded his fear of these situations, convincing him that any moment could expose his vulnerability, which only heightened his sensitivity to potential triggers around him. Each avoidance act, while providing temporary relief, only deepened his feelings of isolation and hopelessness. "His negative appraisal of himself made every act of avoidance feel like a confirmation of his incapacity, feeding into a cycle where the world seemed more threatening and his ability to cope was diminished." He felt the weight of his inaction, believing that he was failing not just himself but also his partner, whom he loved dearly. "This belief further fueled his avoidance, as he became convinced that exposing himself to potential triggers would only highlight his inadequacies, leading him deeper into isolation." This compounded his feelings of shame and unworthiness, reinforcing the deep-seated belief that he was no longer capable of being the husband she deserved. Each time he avoided a potential trigger, he felt guilty, convinced that he was becoming a burden rather than a companion. After months of struggling with these issues, John finally sought help. He had come to realize that the pain of remaining silent was far greater than the fear of confronting his past. Yet, what frightened him most was the possibility that he would never be able to reclaim the person he once was — a capable, compassionate psychologist and a loving husband. In his heart, he clung to a flicker of hope that therapy might help him navigate through the memories that haunted him, allowing him to transform his pain into a path toward healing and reconnection with those he loved. "That thought lingered, and with each encounter, it felt more like an unshakeable truth, leading him to view himself as permanently damaged and vulnerable to the world around him." "Each time he recalled those moments, the belief that he was broken surged, making the memories more vivid and painful, as if they were proof of his irrevocable change." "His negative self-view painted those memories in sharper contrast, causing them to echo in his mind with greater intensity, reinforcing the idea that he was indeed a shadow of his former self." "Those memories became a lens through which he judged himself, each recollection further embedding the notion that he was unworthy of happiness or connection." "This created a feedback loop where the memories only served to validate his fears, leading him to believe that he was spiraling further away from who he used to be." "He had come to recognize that his belief in his brokenness had stifled his ability to seek support, making the act of reaching out a monumental step toward reclaiming his life."
